core.p: **Part (b)**: Explain the importance of poverty **elsewhere in the novella**. In your answer you must consider: how poverty is shown; why it is important to Dickens’s message. You should refer to the context. (20 marks)

essays.q: Explain the importance of poverty elsewhere in the novella.
essays.t: Model essay: poverty and social responsibility
essays.text:
Dickens presents poverty not as the fault of the poor but as the result of the indifference of the rich, and by giving the poor names, faces and families, he turns a political argument into a moral demand that his readers take personal responsibility.

Dickens begins with the attitudes he wants to challenge. In Stave 1, the charity collectors explain that ‘Many thousands are in want of common necessaries’, but Scrooge answers with a list of institutions, ‘Are there no prisons?’ and ‘the Union workhouses?’, believing that his taxes discharge his duty. His wish that the poor should die and ‘decrease the surplus population’ echoes the economist Malthus, whose theory was used in the 1830s and 1840s to justify the harsh Poor Law. Marley’s ghost immediately contradicts him: ‘Mankind was my business’, repeating ‘business’ to redefine what a businessman’s true concerns should be.

Dickens then gives poverty a human face. The Cratchits are poor but dignified: Mrs Cratchit is ‘brave in ribbons, which are cheap and make a goodly show’, and the family greets a small goose as if ‘There never was such a goose’. Their love and gratitude, even Bob’s toast to ‘the Founder of the Feast’, challenge the Victorian belief that the poor were lazy or immoral. Tiny Tim is the novella’s emotional centre: when Scrooge asks whether he will live, the Ghost repeats Scrooge’s own words about the ‘surplus population’, forcing both Scrooge and the reader to see that the ‘surplus’ is a real child. Dickens, who had read the 1843 Children’s Employment Commission report, uses this sentiment deliberately to move readers.

The warnings are stark. Beneath the Ghost’s robe, the children Ignorance and Want are ‘wretched, abject, frightful, hideous, miserable’, an allegory of the products of neglect. The Ghost warns ‘most of all beware this boy’, reflecting Dickens’s belief, strengthened by his visit to the Field Lane Ragged School, that lack of education would lead society to ‘Doom’. Stave 4 shows poverty’s darker side too: in Old Joe’s shop, the poor sell the dead man’s possessions, suggesting that neglect breeds desperation and crime.

Finally, Dickens shows what responsibility looks like. In Stave 5, Scrooge gives the charity collector a sum with ‘a great many back-payments’ included, raises Bob’s salary and becomes ‘a second father’ to Tiny Tim. The solution Dickens offers is personal and practical: not reliance on institutions, but generosity from those who can afford it. By ending with Tiny Tim’s blessing, ‘God bless Us, Every One!’, he includes all classes in a single community, leaving his readers with the clear message that the poor are their business.
essays.thesis: Dickens presents poverty not as the fault of the poor but as the result of the indifference of the rich, and by giving the poor names, faces and families, he turns a political argument into a moral demand that his readers take personal responsibility.
why: **AO1**: a conceptual argument (indifference of the rich; personal responsibility).
**AO3**: Malthus, Poor Law, Children’s Employment Commission, Ragged Schools, all tied to text.

exam.q: Practice: write a conclusion evaluating whether Dickens’s solution (personal charity) is enough.

mistakes.r: Discuss attitudes to poverty and Dickens’s solution as well.

summary: A full grade 9 part (b) model essay on poverty and social responsibility, showing how Dickens moves readers from Scrooge’s cold attitudes to personal, practical charity.

terms.d: The duty of individuals to help others.
